prompt.context: Our client, a private equity firm, is considering acquiring a company that manufactures traditional toys. Toy Co., the potential acquisition, was founded in 1923 and is one of the world's largest traditional toy makers. The traditional toy industry is dominated by several large players and Toy Co. is one of the top three players by sales volume in the space. We have been hired to evaluate Toy Co.'s current strategy and to determine whether the private equity firm should place a bid to acquire the company.
prompt.question: What considerations should the PE firm make in determining whether or not to acquire Toy Co.?

clarifying_info.q: What is the selling price of Toy Co.?
clarifying_info.a: The selling price of Toy Co. is irrelevant to the case discussion.

clarifying_info.q: Are there other firms interested in acquiring Toy Co.?
clarifying_info.a: We have no information about other firms interested in acquiring and should assume there are none.

exhibits.title: Traditional Toy Sales, 2005-2016
exhibits.shows: A bar or stacked chart showing annual sales in dollars for four traditional toy varieties (Dolls, Action Figures, Outdoor Games, Blocks and Puzzles) from 2005 to 2016, with a note indicating 2% industry CAGR. The y-axis runs from $0 to $7,000,000,000.

framework: Potential Acquisition / Toy Co. analysis: Economics (revenue streams by toy variety, price per toy, number and breakdown of customers; costs including materials and labor; distribution channels)
Market analysis: Competition (new entrants and long-time rivals); Customer preferences (rise of electronics)
Exit opportunities: Potential buyers; Exit multiples
PE context: The firm will be interested only if it can turn around Toy Co. and sell at a profit — always frame recommendations for the PE firm, not Toy Co. directly

questions.prompt: Question 1: How would you estimate the annual sales volume of toys in the U.S.?
questions.guidance: Segment the U.S. population into buyer groups. A strong candidate will identify: older children, adult toy enthusiasts, parents, and grandparents. The interviewer may provide population sizes after the candidate does initial estimations, then provide purchase rates and cart size per group. The candidate should multiply population × purchases per year × cart size for each segment and sum.

math.setup: For each buyer segment: Market Size = Population × Purchases per Year × Cart Size
math.answer: $14.4 billion annual U.S. toy market (assumes ~100 million U.S. households as the base)

questions.prompt: Question 2 (Exhibit 1): Explain the chart. How has the market share of each toy variety changed over the past decade? What societal trends could have caused these shifts?
questions.guidance: Candidate should read the exhibit, identify directional trends for each category, and link them to real-world societal drivers. Strong answers quantify some shifts in either raw dollars or share points.

math.setup: Market share by variety for selected years (from exhibit data table)
steps: Blocks and Puzzles: 15% (2005) → 11% (2016) — declined ~4 percentage points
math.answer: Action Figures gained the most share; Dolls lost the most share; Outdoor Games saw moderate growth; Blocks and Puzzles declined modestly.

questions.prompt: Question 3 (Brainstorm): Based on your analysis of Exhibit 1, what recommendations would you make to Toy Co. to better position its offerings to match consumer trends?
questions.guidance: Tests both creative brainstorming and structured organization. Candidate should address each toy category with specific strategic actions tied to the trend data.

brainstorming.prompt: Based on the Exhibit 1 market share trends, what specific strategic recommendations would you make to Toy Co. for each toy category?

categories.name: Action Figures
ideas: Partner with movie studios or TV shows to build a robust arsenal of characters
Focus on female character action figures to capture share from declining dolls category

categories.name: Dolls
ideas: Focus on modern dolls portraying powerful female characters
Follow the model of Barbie's introduction of dolls with diverse races, heights, and body types
Adjust production volume downward as segment has seen the greatest decline

categories.name: Outdoor Games
ideas: Expand offerings to capture the push toward healthy living and screen-free play
Capitalize on parental preference for outdoor activities

categories.name: Blocks and Puzzles / Electronics
ideas: This segment has declined due to electronics and video games
Toy Co. can consider launching electronic versions of classic games
Explore entering the non-traditional toy space as a growth avenue

recommendation: YES — the PE firm should consider acquiring: there is movement in a growing (2% CAGR) industry, and under strong management Toy Co. can earn an even stronger market position by repositioning toward action figures and outdoor games.

NO — the PE firm may pass: a 2% industry CAGR is not compelling for a PE return profile, and electronics will continue to encroach on traditional toy market share. Either stance is defensible as long as the candidate frames it from the PE firm's perspective (ability to acquire, turn around, and exit at a profit).
risks: As a legacy retailer, Toy Co. may resist new ownership and fail to implement recommendations
Electronics will continue to grow and erode market share from traditional toys
Movie studios may begin manufacturing their own toys, causing Toy Co. to lose significant business in the action figure space
next_steps: Gain a full understanding of Toy Co.'s financials (only the traditional toy market was analyzed in this case) to determine whether it is the best acquisition target in the space
Begin planning how Toy Co.'s production can respond to different market trends identified in the analysis
